title: Pilgrimage
hookLine: traveling to a holy place as prayer

lines: THEY DON'T WANT THE ROAD TO END.
cards: Two friends are walking out of Jerusalem on a Sunday, heading for a village called Emmaus. Their feet hurt, and their hearts hurt worse.

The man they had hoped in has been crucified, and now there are strange reports of an empty tomb. A stranger falls into step and asks what they're talking about. They stop, faces sad, and tell him everything.
Then, as they walk, he opens the scriptures to them, step after step. They don't know who he is. They only know they don't want the road to end.

teach.h: JESUS'S FAMILY WENT UP EACH YEAR.
teach.b: A pilgrimage is a journey to a holy place, made as prayer. Not tourism with a church stop: the trip itself is the point. The habit runs through scripture.

Luke's Gospel says Jesus's parents went up to Jerusalem every year for the Passover, and took him along when he was twelve. Tradition hears some of the Psalms as songs for pilgrims going up to the Temple.
One opens, in the Douay-Rheims, "I rejoiced at the things that were said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord."

teach.h: A PICTURE OF THE WHOLE JOURNEY.
teach.b: The Catechism says pilgrimages evoke our earthly journey toward heaven, and are traditionally special times for renewal in prayer. So the road is a picture.

Every pilgrim acts out, with their legs, what the Catechism says about the whole of life: we're on the way, not yet home. Back at Emmaus, the friends press the stranger to stay, since evening is coming.
At table he takes bread, blesses it and breaks it, and their eyes are opened. He vanishes.

teach.h: OUR HEART BURNING, IN THE WAY.
teach.b: And they say to each other, "Was not our heart burning within us, whilst he spoke in the way?" In the way: on the road, before they knew.
Last, the Church calls herself a pilgrim.

teach.h: WE SHALL GO INTO THE HOUSE OF THE LORD.
teach.b: The Second Vatican Council speaks of the pilgrim Church on earth. A pilgrimage to a shrine is a small version of that bigger walk, done on purpose, with tired feet.

how: Catholics make pilgrimages to shrines near and far, often in parish groups, with Mass, confession and prayer along the way; some walk the whole route on foot.

o: a church tour taken while on vacation
a vow to stay in one monastery for life
a journey to a holy place, made as prayer

p: two friends walking with a stranger
went up to Jerusalem for Passover
a picture of the journey to heaven

s: a pilgrimage is a trip where you visit a church at the end
the journey itself is part of the prayer, not just the arrival.
the two friends on the road to Emmaus knew Jesus right away
they knew him at the table, when he broke the bread. then they remembered their hearts burning on the road.
the Catechism says pilgrimages evoke our earthly journey toward heaven
it calls them traditionally special times for renewal in prayer.

games.q: you're one of the two walking to Emmaus. you reach the village at dusk, and the stranger acts as if he's going farther. what do you do?
o: press him to stay, since it's getting dark.
walk on with him to the next town.
games.why: they urge him to stay because evening is coming. at table he breaks the bread, and they finally know him.

practice: Picture the nearest church you could reach on foot, and the walk there: which street first, and what you'd pass, a bakery, a school, a bus stop full of people.
Decide that the walk itself will be the prayer, no headphones, no hurry, and a minute's sit when you arrive. If you pray, say a Hail Mary at each corner; if you don't, just notice every step.

wordCard.voice: Pilgrimage. A journey to a holy place, made as prayer, in which the road itself becomes part of the prayer. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: a journey abroad, a stay in a foreign land; the Church's word for pilgrimage.

carryVoice: Your line: the road is the prayer. The arrival counts, and so does every step before it. See you tomorrow.
